paras: The Coffeeville riot of 1880 was a street fight in Coffeeville, Yalobusha County, Mississippi, on August 21, 1880, between R. V. Pearson, the Greenback candidate for sheriff, and Spearman, a Black man marching in a Democratic procession. Early wire reports said Pearson killed Spearman instantly and was himself shot dead, but later Mississippi reports had Spearman only slightly wounded and Pearson recovering to win the sheriff's election three days later. Democratic and Greenback papers blamed each other's side for starting it.

A special election for sheriff was set for Tuesday, August 24, with Pearson opposing the Democrat, Captain Z. D. Jennings. Spearman, the county's "colored Republican Election Commissioner," had published a card on August 19 denying Greenback charges that he had been "bought by the Democratic party" and backing Jennings.

On August 21 the Democrats held a ratification meeting and pole-raising at Coffeeville, and the Greenbackers met in town the same day. A New Orleans Press special said the Greenbackers took the court-house where the Democrats had expected to speak; Greenback chairman A. T. Wimberly said his party met outside town.

About three o'clock the Democratic clubs, led by a Grenada brass band, met the Greenback clubs on Depot street. There, according to the Democratic-side reports, Pearson "struck and shot" Spearman, and the men in the front rank of the procession joined the fight. A volley of shots was fired at Pearson, who was hit three times, once in the shoulder and twice in the legs, and was carried into a store for treatment. R. B. Riddick and R. C. Kelly were also wounded; local reports placed them at the head of the Democratic procession, the Memphis wire among Pearson's friends.
Black onlookers "fled like scared sheep," stores closed, and armed men filled the streets until a militia call to Grenada was countermanded and the town grew quiet.

Governor Stone and Secretary of State Henry C. Myers arrived the next day, found the town quiet, and complimented Captain R. H. Wyatt of the Coffeeville Guards and Mayor Ross. Pearson survived and won the special election on August 24 by a majority of 73, and the Greenback Yalobusha Standard reported him "rapidly improving." No report of an arrest, inquest or prosecution for any of the shootings appears in the coverage.

Wimberly wrote that two days later armed Democrats from several counties gathered at Coffeeville and that committees told him to give up the Greenback cause or be killed. On September 12 a "colored man, late of Yalobusha county," signing as R. W. Spearman, wrote from Fort Scott, Kansas, that "The Greenback mob" had driven him from his home for supporting the Republican party and Jennings.

The story spread through a Memphis dispatch of August 22, gathered from train passengers, which the New York Sun headed "Riot in Coffeeville, Miss." and "The Greenback Candidate for Sheriff Shooting a Democratic Negro." It also ran as "Fatal Political Fight" in the Daily Gazette and "Bloody Riot" in the Dallas Daily Herald. The Canton American Citizen headlined "A Greenback Candidate Kills a Democratic Negro" before adding that Pearson had lived, and the Jackson Comet printed the governor-endorsed account as "A Correct Report," appending Spearman's card to "explain the cause of the difficulty."

The Silver State of Unionville, Nevada, called the shooting "An Unnoticed Outrage" and charged that the Republican press passed over it "because the victim was a colored Democrat." Greenback-leaning and Republican papers reversed the story: the Chicago Tribune printed Wimberly's charge of a deliberate attempt at murder, the Chillicothe Crisis wrote of "a deep laid scheme to murder Pearson," and the Somerset Press repeated his claim that Democrats had hired Spearman.

Accounts disagreed over who began the fight: Democratic-side reports said Pearson attacked Spearman, and the Silver State said the Black man "ran against" the candidate. Wimberly said Spearman insulted Pearson, who punched him with an umbrella, and that Spearman and about six Democrats then shot Pearson; the Chillicothe Crisis had Spearman shooting back and escaping before the procession fired.

The Memphis wire had Spearman killed instantly, the New Orleans Press special shot in the neck, and the Coffeeville reports slightly wounded. The local reports were closer to the event, and the wire that reported his death also wrongly reported Pearson's.

reader.title: Coffeeville riot of 1880
bases: A street fight between rival white party factions in which a Black man in the Democratic procession and the white Greenback candidate exchanged violence and the candidate was then shot by Democratic marchers; no mob attack on Black people is reported (A1, A8, A9, A17).

Many reports agree that Pearson and Spearman clashed and Pearson was shot on Aug. 21, but Democratic-side reports have Pearson attacking Spearman (A8, A9) while Greenback accounts have Spearman provoking Pearson and shooting him (A14, A17), and Spearman's injuries range from death (A1) to a slight wound (A9) to none (A14).

accounts.label: Memphis wire (train passengers)
accounts.gist: Pearson shot Spearman, a Black man in the Democratic procession, killing him instantly; a volley was fired at Pearson, who died that night.

accounts.label: Coffeeville specials (Democratic side, endorsed by Gov. Stone)
accounts.gist: Pearson attacked Spearman, the colored Republican election commissioner; shots were exchanged, Pearson was seriously and Spearman slightly wounded, and two Democratic marchers were drawn in.

accounts.label: New Orleans Press special
accounts.gist: For 'some unknown reason' Pearson struck and shot Spearman, who was shot in the neck and whose whereabouts were unknown; front-rank marchers joined in and Pearson was shot three times.

accounts.label: Greenback chairman Wimberly
accounts.gist: Democrats hired Spearman; he insulted Pearson, who punched him with an umbrella, and Spearman and a half dozen Democrats shot Pearson down in a deliberate attempt at murder.

accounts.label: Greenback exchange (Chillicothe Crisis)
accounts.gist: Spearman accosted Pearson, was struck with an umbrella, shot back and escaped around a corner; the Democratic procession then fired on Pearson.

framing.detail: Wire versions headlined the case as a riot in which 'The Greenback Candidate for Sheriff' shot 'a Democratic Negro' ('Fatal Political Fight', 'Bloody Riot').
Mississippi Democratic papers blamed Pearson, printed the governor-endorsed 'Correct Report' and Spearman's card as the cause, while noting Pearson had survived and won.
The Silver State's 'An Unnoticed Outrage' condemned the shooting of 'a colored Democrat' and accused the Republican press of ignoring it.
The Chicago Tribune, Chillicothe Crisis and Somerset Press condemned the shooting of Pearson as a Democratic plot and cast Spearman as a provocateur.
